Hi, I'm Monisha!

I'm a multidisciplinary Product Designer with a background in architecture and a master's in Human-Computer Interaction and Design from Indiana University Bloomington. My journey from designing physical spaces to digital experiences has shaped how I approach design—combining spatial thinking, user research, and a systems perspective to create intuitive, meaningful products.

Today, I work at the intersection of design, strategy, and technology, turning complex problems into simple, human-centered solutions. From interfaces to AI-powered tools, I love bringing ideas to life while balancing form, function, and impact.

Originally from Bangalore and now based in NYC, I enjoy collaborating across disciplines, exploring new ideas, and creating experiences that make a difference.

How I work

Human first

I design for different abilities, contexts, and levels of confidence, with clarity and accessibility built into the experience.

Stay curious

I ask questions early and use research to check whether we're solving the right problem.

Make complexity clear

I simplify workflows and interactions while keeping the detail people need to make confident decisions.

Keep learning

I adapt to feedback, new evidence, and changing constraints, treating each iteration as a chance to improve.

What I bring to a team

User research

I turn interviews, usability tests, and feedback into clear design decisions.

Product thinking

I connect user needs, business goals, and technical constraints to help the team decide what to build.

Design systems

I build reusable components and interaction patterns that keep interfaces consistent as products grow.

Collaboration

I work with product, engineering, and stakeholders to share context, resolve trade-offs, and move ideas into implementation.

Outside work

Away from my desk, you'll usually find me at the piano, lost in a book, or out on a hiking trail.

I love noticing the small details—with a camera in hand, exploring somewhere new, or taking a quick escape to the beach.
